title: Comprehensive assessment of scale formation, corrosion, and biological pollution in a cooling water supply system
author: Biedunkova, Kuznietsov, et al.

steps.title: Collect water samples
steps.instruction: Collect representative cooling‑water samples from the CWS at the RNPP for physicochemical and biological analysis.

steps.title: Determine physicochemical parameters
steps.instruction: Measure pH, temperature, dissolved‑salt concentration, chloride, total hardness and total alkalinity according to the standard methods cited in reference [1]. Record all values.

steps.title: Calculate scaling and corrosion indices
steps.instruction: Using the measured physicochemical data, calculate the φ‑ψ, LSI and RSI indices. Report the observed ranges: φ‑ψ = ‑0.91 to 3.61 (M = 0.245 ± 0.521), LSI = 0.02 to 2.22 (M = 1.56 ± 0.381), RSI = 4.17 to 7.95 (M = 5.54 ± 0.58). Note the strong negative correlation between LSI and RSI (ρ = ‑0.9635).

steps.title: Prepare test‑bench specimens
steps.instruction: Select three witness samples of St‑20 carbon steel (C = 0.16–0.24 %) and two heating‑element specimens. Clean, dry and weigh each specimen (record initial masses W1 for steel and M0 for heating elements).

steps.title: Assemble test bench
steps.instruction: Install the three steel witness samples and two heating elements on the bench shown in Fig. 3, positioning them downstream of the heat exchanger to simulate pipeline conditions. Connect the system to the cooling‑water loop and set the water temperature to 45 °C.

steps.title: Run bench test
steps.instruction: Operate the bench continuously for 800 h, maintaining constant flow and temperature. Ensure that external variables (temperature spikes, flow turbulence) are minimized.

steps.title: Measure post‑test masses
steps.instruction: After 800 h, remove the specimens, gently rinse to remove loose deposits, and weigh the steel samples again (record W2) and the heating elements (record M1).

steps.title: Calculate corrosion rate V
steps.instruction: Compute the corrosion rate using V = K·(W1‑W2)/(F·t·g) where K = 87.6, F is the specimen surface area, t = 800 h and g is the metal density. Report the observed range 0.25–0.35 g · m⁻²·h⁻¹ (M = 0.305 ± 0.022). Verify that V does not exceed the standard limit of 0.5 g · m⁻²·h⁻¹.

steps.title: Calculate scale formation rate S
steps.instruction: Compute the scale formation rate using S = (M0‑M1)/(F·t). Report the observed range 0.52–0.75 g · m⁻²·h⁻¹ (M = 0.63 ± 0.08).

steps.title: Inspect specimens for deposits and biofilm
steps.instruction: Photograph the steel samples before testing, after testing, and after removal of deposits. Note the presence of surface deposits and any biofilm; confirm that no localized corrosion is visible after deposit removal.

steps.title: Determine colony‑forming units (CFU)
steps.instruction: Using the Orion test system, plate water samples on agar and incubate under standard conditions. Count colonies and express results as CFU · cm⁻³. Expected range: 10³–10⁷ CFU · cm⁻³ (M = 10⁴ ± 10³).

steps.title: Count algae cells
steps.instruction: Place a known volume of water in the exposure chamber, observe under a microscope and count yellow‑green (Tribonema) and green (Ladophora glomerata) algae. Report the concentration as cells · cm⁻³; expected range 300 000–400 000 cells · cm⁻³ (M = 348 000 ± 20 000).

steps.title: Monitor invertebrate fouling with hydrobox
steps.instruction: Install the hydrobox (cylindrical container with plexiglass plates) in the water flow line. After a defined exposure period, retrieve the hydrobox, inspect the internal plates and count retained invertebrates (e.g., molluscs, snails). Record numbers for further assessment.

steps.title: Compare results to standards
steps.instruction: Evaluate corrosion rate V against the limit of 0.5 g · m⁻²·h⁻¹, scale formation S against operational criteria, and biological indicators (CFU, algae cells, invertebrate counts) against the need for biocidal treatment as indicated in references [6,18]. Document any required corrective actions.
